source.author: Al Brooks
source.chapter_title: “Reversal” Patterns: Double Tops and Bottoms and Head and Shoulders Tops and Bottoms

conventions: stop entries mechanized as signal-bar-close then next-bar-open; every tunable constant is a parameter; long side only in pseudocode

candidates.name: DoubleTopBottomPattern
candidates.quote: There was a large double top in the monthly Standard & Poor's (S&P) cash index... The standard entry of a double top is on a sell stop just below the low of the dip between the two tops.
candidates.description: A double top is two swing highs at approximately the same price separated by a pullback low (the 'dip'); a double bottom is the mirror image, two swing lows separated by a pullback high. Shared primitive for this chapter.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification used as a signal precondition)

complexity.reason: needs swing-pivot detection and a price-proximity comparison between two non-adjacent pivots with a pullback structure between them

notes: The book's own thesis is that double tops usually behave as continuation patterns, not reversals; this candidate is the pure pattern-recognition primitive, kept separate from the trading decision (see R20-05/R20-06).

candidates.name: DoubleTopBreakoutShortEntry
candidates.quote: The standard entry of a double top is on a sell stop just below the low of the dip between the two tops. However, that is rarely successful because 80 percent of breakouts fail.
candidates.description: The book's standard (literal) double-top entry: sell stop one tick below the low of the pullback dip between the two tops.
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the dip low

complexity.reason: inherits R20-01's pivot-based pattern detection; the stop-entry arithmetic itself is trivial

notes: Brooks explicitly says this literal breakout entry succeeds only about 20% of the time; recorded as the book's stated rule, not as a recommendation -- see R20-05/R20-06 for the more reliable continuation-based alternative.

candidates.name: HeadAndShouldersPattern
candidates.quote: They are wedges because they have three pushes down, one after the left shoulder, a second after the head, and the third after the right shoulder.
candidates.description: A head-and-shoulders top is a three-push pattern (a specialization of the wedge/three-push primitive) whose middle push (the head) is more extreme than the two outer pushes (the shoulders), which are roughly equal to each other; a neckline connects the two pullback lows between the shoulders and head. A head-and-shoulders bottom is the mirror.
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (pattern classification used as a signal precondition)

complexity.reason: specializes the already-hard three-push wedge primitive with a shoulder-symmetry test and a neckline drawn through two pivot lows

notes: Depends on R18-01 (ThreePushWedgePattern, chapter 18): the book treats head-and-shoulders as functionally the same as a wedge or triangle.

candidates.name: HeadAndShouldersNecklineBreakoutEntry
candidates.quote: if there is a head and shoulders top in a bull market, a breakout below the neckline will usually fail
candidates.description: The standard (literal) head-and-shoulders entry: sell stop one tick below the neckline for a top, buy stop one tick above the neckline for a bottom.
candidates.pseudocode:
isValidShortStopEntry = open[0] > (necklinePrice - entryTick) && low[0] <= (necklinePrice - entryTick);
enterShortAtStop = isHeadAndShouldersTop[1] && isValidShortStopEntry;
candidates.book_order_type: sell stop one tick below the neckline

complexity.reason: inherits R20-03's pivot/neckline detection; the stop-entry arithmetic itself is trivial

notes: Per the chapter's thesis, this breakout usually fails; see R20-05 for the with-trend failure-continuation entry the book actually recommends.

candidates.name: FailedReversalPatternContinuationEntry
candidates.quote: a breakout below the neckline will usually fail and the market will most likely then reverse up and have a with-trend breakout to the upside, above the right shoulder.
candidates.description: When a double-top/bottom or head-and-shoulders pattern forms as a pause within an established larger trend and its countertrend breakout (the double-top dip-low break, or the head-and-shoulders neckline break) fails to follow through -- price closes back through the breakout level within a few bars -- enter with the larger trend on that failure, since these 'reversal' patterns are actually continuation patterns far more often than not.
candidates.book_order_type: buy stop one tick above the failed-breakout signal bar's high

complexity.reason: needs the underlying pattern/neckline detection, a tracked prior breakout level and bar index, and an established-larger-trend context that this chapter does not itself define

notes: This is the chapter's central, most distinctive idea: treat 'reversal' patterns as continuation patterns and trade the failure of their countertrend breakout, not the breakout itself.

candidates.name: AvoidNaiveReversalPatternCountertrendEntry
candidates.quote: It is a mistake to see every top or bottom as a great reversal setup, because if you take all of those countertrend entries, the majority of your trades will be losers... However, if you are selective and look for other evidence that a trend might reverse, these can be effective setups.
candidates.description: Because double tops/bottoms and head-and-shoulders patterns are trading ranges that continue the larger trend far more often than they reverse it, do not take every countertrend breakout of one of these patterns (R20-02/R20-04); only take it when there is additional selective evidence that the trend might actually reverse.
candidates.pseudocode:
// research: 'other evidence' that a trend might reverse is left undefined in this chapter
allowCountertrendReversalEntry = (isDoubleTop[0] || isHeadAndShouldersTop[0]) && reversalConfidenceScore[0] >= reversalConfidenceThreshold;
candidates.book_order_type: n/a (gates whether R20-02/R20-04 may be taken at all)

complexity.reason: "other evidence that a trend might reverse" has no stated bar-level test; a design decision is needed before this can be coded

candidates.name: ReversalPatternHeightMeasuredMoveTarget
candidates.quote: This would then be followed by a breakout of the top of the pattern and an approximate measured move up over the next decade or two.
candidates.description: After a with-trend breakout of a double-top/bottom or head-and-shoulders continuation pattern, project a measured-move target equal to the pattern's height (its highest extreme to its lowest extreme) added from the breakout point.
candidates.book_order_type: limit exit (or discretionary scale-out) at the measured-move price

complexity.reason: pattern-height extremes require the same pivot detection as R20-01/R20-03; the projection arithmetic itself is trivial

notes: Same measured-move family as R18-08 (TwoLegMeasuredMoveExit, chapter 18) but the height source is the whole pattern's range rather than a single leg; likely mergeable with a generic measured-move exit primitive.

rejected.quote: The cause is obviously much more complicated than this because there are countless participants acting for countless reasons, but this is a component.
rejected.reason: pure discretion / market narrative, no bar-level test proposed

chapter_summary: Chapter 20 argues that double tops/bottoms and head-and-shoulders tops/bottoms are almost always continuation patterns (wedges/triangles in disguise) that only rarely produce a genuine reversal, so their textbook breakout entries (sell stop below the double-top dip, or below the H&S neckline) usually fail, and the higher-probability trade is to buy (or sell) the failure of that breakout back in the direction of the larger trend. Candidates split into the two pattern-recognition primitives (double top/bottom, head-and-shoulders, the latter depending on chapter 18's wedge primitive), their literal textbook breakout entries, the book's actual recommended failed-breakout continuation entry, a selectivity filter against naive countertrend entries, and a pattern-height measured-move exit. Only 2 pages / 3 figures, mostly one long worked example (the S&P monthly chart) plus general thesis; page 131 carries almost all of the extractable content.
